schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file outside the working directory that you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. browser-use <<'PY'

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

## zotero-research
Read-only access to the user's Zotero research library. For substantive sport-science questions, build a Zotero-first evidence pack before answering. Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

# HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games

**What it is** — Across the case studies, high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is not just dosed up session to session, it is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). From around mid-rehab (session 5 in Case 1, session 3 in Case 2), HSR shifts to short interval formats: "10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, or 15 seconds on and off" (Case 1, ~10:17-10:35), and "short interval, high intensity interval training formats, like 10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 20 seconds on, 20 seconds off" (Case 2, ~23:14-23:22). From around session 7-8, small-sided games and technical/tactical drills start to contribute HSR/VHSR "a little bit more meaningfully" or "more organically," alongside whatever prescribed running work continues (Case 1, ~10:35-10:46; Case 2, ~23:25-23:30). A similar shift to small-sided games shows up in Case 4, a knee-joint case kept straight-line-only through session 6 for bracing reasons: "small-sided games, so modified rehab specific drills and also partial participation with the team" began at session 8 (~41:34-41:40). Harries reports a separate, linear VHSR/sprint increase from sessions 4-8 in the same passage (~41:43-41:46) without explicitly linking the two statements, so this case supports the format shift itself but not a stated causal link to VHSR volume.

**Why it works** — Harries does not give an explicit mechanism for why the delivery format itself should shift (his only nearby general statement is that session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding," said of the mid-rehab checkpoint, not this format shift specifically, ~20:08-20:14). Inference (entry writer's): moving from individually-prescribed, fixed-distance repeats to short intervals to game-based drills lets the athlete accumulate the same category of high-speed exposure in progressively less predictable, more sport-representative contexts, without needing to represcribe every rep once basic mechanics and pacing are established.

**When to apply** — Use as the default organizing structure for programming HSR/VHSR volume across an on-field rehab block, once basic linear mechanics and pacing are established (roughly Level 1-2, see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP protocol of its own yet; this three-stage shift is a directly transferable structure to pair with Baylor's own GPS velocity-band thresholds.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed session-count rule; the session numbers cited here (5, 3, 7, 8) are case-specific, not a stated formula, and the source's own repeated caveat is that the framework is a guide adjusted to context, not a step-by-step protocol (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]). The Case 4 example also shows the shift can run alongside other, unrelated restrictions (change-of-direction was still withheld through session 6 there for bracing reasons); do not treat "small-sided games by session 7-8" as evidence that all restrictions lift on that same timeline. Do not import a specific case's session numbers as a prescription.

**Example** — In [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]], HSR moved from 100 m repeats (session 2, which overshot the low 17 km/h threshold, see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]) to short intervals (session 3) to small-sided games contributing HSR organically (session 8).

# Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — As a returning athlete moves from an isolated running-only schedule into overlapping with team training, Harries shapes each week of rehab around the team's own weekly training rhythm, not a fixed rehab-only calendar. Case 2: "by week three, we started to fall into the team's training structure a bit more" (~17:40-17:44): a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:45-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 4 (knee), week 5: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into the larger session planned at the end of week 6 (~37:24-37:46). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review: Applied Performance "already undulate[s] load across the team week," and this pattern is proposed as "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern" (Review and Plan, line 75) - i.e. the existing team-week undulation is the natural anchor for this on-field-rehab pattern, not a separate structure to invent.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. None of it is validated against outcome data beyond what happened in each case being reported without a stated recurrence. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], weeks 5-7, for the clearest stated rationale: a frequency cut used as a deliberate bridge to a larger session, and an RTP week deliberately matched to the team's normal in-season training rhythm.

# The Mid-Rehab Checkpoint: ~85% MV Around Day 10-14 for Hamstring-Type Injuries

**What it is** — Harries gives a calendar anchor, matched to force-production, reactive-strength and healing-time criteria that line up with the general 75-85% MV gate (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]), for hamstring-type strain injuries specifically. Describing session 5 (stated as "identical to session five in case one," ~19:47-19:56), he says it "probably represents a typical mid stage max velocity progression for this type of injury at about the 10 [to] 14 day post injury mark" (~19:56-20:04) and, discussing the same session a few lines later, that it "typifies the point in rehab where you push towards around about 85% max velocity at that day 14 type mark, plus or minus, but rarely would you go beyond that. Most would consider this a bit of a sound ceiling until further force production or reactive strength criteria are confirmed, as well as some adequate time for biological healing" (~20:40-21:02). He adds that the session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding" (~20:08-20:14). The transcript literally reads "10 day 14 post injury mark," almost certainly an ASR-dropped "to"; read as "10 to 14 day."

**Why it works** — Same underlying rationale as the general gate: Harries treats ~85% MV as a workable interim ceiling pending confirmation of force-production and reactive-strength criteria, plus adequate healing time, not as evidence that higher intensity would be unsafe. He gives no physiological mechanism for why day 10-14 specifically is the natural point for this pause; the timing is presented as his stated clinical experience ("most would consider," "typical"), not a derived rule.

**When to apply** — As a rough calendar anchor for planning when a hamstring-type strain rehab should reach the 75-85% MV gate, so force-production and reactive-strength testing (Nordic, isometric benchmarks, hop test; see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]) can be scheduled around day 10-14 rather than left open-ended. # The Five-Element Case-Review Structure

**What it is** — Harries reviews each of his four case studies through the same five elements, stated explicitly: "the rehab timeline, which is a high-level overview of the return to play calendar"; "the loading structure. So how was loading planned and how was it progressed across on-field rehab"; "the progression of maximum velocity and how those linear running intensities were increased"; "our multi-directional speed and agility progressions and how we developed acceleration, deceleration and change of direction"; and "for each case study... the sport-specific skill progressions and how the technical and tactical tasks were integrated" (~00:39-01:17). He also states the cases were deliberately chosen to minimize individual complexity so the framework's application would read clearly, while acknowledging "no case is ever entirely free from complexity" (~01:21-01:45), and that he included cases that "didn't go perfect to show that the real world is not always that way" (~01:45-01:51).

**Why it works** — No stated mechanism; this is a presentation and documentation structure Harries uses for teaching, not a claim about rehab physiology or efficacy.

# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase

**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).

**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. 103	# HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games
104	
105	**What it is** — Across the case studies, high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is not just dosed up session to session, it is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). From around mid-rehab (session 5 in Case 1, session 3 in Case 2), HSR shifts to short interval formats: "10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, or 15 seconds on and off" (Case 1, ~10:17-10:35), and "short interval, high intensity interval training formats, like 10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 20 seconds on, 20 seconds off" (Case 2, ~23:14-23:22). From around session 7-8, small-sided games and technical/tactical drills start to contribute HSR/VHSR "a little bit more meaningfully" or "more organically," alongside whatever prescribed running work continues (Case 1, ~10:35-10:46; Case 2, ~23:25-23:30). A similar shift to small-sided games shows up in Case 4, a knee-joint case kept straight-line-only through session 6 for bracing reasons: "small-sided games, so modified rehab specific drills and also partial participation with the team" began at session 8 (~41:34-41:40). Harries reports a separate, linear VHSR/sprint increase from sessions 4-8 in the same passage (~41:43-41:46) without explicitly linking the two statements, so this case supports the format shift itself but not a stated causal link to VHSR volume.
106	
107	**Why it works** — Harries does not give an explicit mechanism for why the delivery format itself should shift (his only nearby general statement is that session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding," said of the mid-rehab checkpoint, not this format shift specifically, ~20:08-20:14). Inference (entry writer's): moving from individually-prescribed, fixed-distance repeats to short intervals to game-based drills lets the athlete accumulate the same category of high-speed exposure in progressively less predictable, more sport-representative contexts, without needing to represcribe every rep once basic mechanics and pacing are established.
108	
109	**When to apply** — Use as the default organizing structure for programming HSR/VHSR volume across an on-field rehab block, once basic linear mechanics and pacing are established (roughly Level 1-2, see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP protocol of its own yet; this three-stage shift is a directly transferable structure to pair with Baylor's own GPS velocity-band thresholds.
110	
111	**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed session-count rule; the session numbers cited here (5, 3, 7, 8) are case-specific, not a stated formula, and the source's own repeated caveat is that the framework is a guide adjusted to context, not a step-by-step protocol (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]). 184	# The Five-Element Case-Review Structure
185	
186	**What it is** — Harries reviews each of his four case studies through the same five elements, stated explicitly: "the rehab timeline, which is a high-level overview of the return to play calendar"; "the loading structure. So how was loading planned and how was it progressed across on-field rehab"; "the progression of maximum velocity and how those linear running intensities were increased"; "our multi-directional speed and agility progressions and how we developed acceleration, deceleration and change of direction"; and "for each case study... the sport-specific skill progressions and how the technical and tactical tasks were integrated" (~00:39-01:17). He also states the cases were deliberately chosen to minimize individual complexity so the framework's application would read clearly, while acknowledging "no case is ever entirely free from complexity" (~01:21-01:45), and that he included cases that "didn't go perfect to show that the real world is not always that way" (~01:45-01:51).
187	
188	**Why it works** — No stated mechanism; this is a presentation and documentation structure Harries uses for teaching, not a claim about rehab physiology or efficacy.
189	
190	**When to apply** — As a template for a Baylor RTP case log or after-action review: for a returning athlete, record (1) the RTP timeline/calendar, (2) the loading structure and how it was progressed, (3) max-velocity progression, (4) MDSA progression, and (5) sport-skill progression. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates "do not yet exist" at Applied Performance and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work; this five-element structure is a ready-made scaffold specifically for RTP case documentation, distinct from that broader reporting gap.
191	
192	**When NOT to apply** — This is a presentation structure built for four selected, deliberately simplified cases, not a validated clinical documentation standard, and Harries does not claim it captures everything relevant to an actual RTP decision. It has no explicit slot for the competitive-exposure/hesitation criteria in [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] and [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]] (those show up folded into the sport-skill-progression element in practice, not as their own listed element). Do not treat the five elements as exhaustive without adding Baylor's own required documentation fields (medical clearance sign-off, testing-battery results, incident/mechanism detail) alongside them.
193	
194	**Example** — Each of the four case-study entries in this folder roughly follows this order in its own body sections (rehab timeline folded into "What it is," then MV progression, MDSA, sport-specific skill as separate paragraphs), though none names the structure explicitly and none gives "loading structure" its own separate paragraph the way Harries' five-element list implies; see [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for the closest match.
195	
196	**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]; [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] (reciprocal link suggestion: each could add "documented using [[framework--five-element-case-review-structure]]" to its own Related line)

210	
211	# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase
212	
213	**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).
214	
215	**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Harries' own stated reason is narrower: the middle-phase time is set "to equate to a given speed through that middle distance... that's going to correspond to the athlete's max velocity" (~18:18-18:29) - i.e. it gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity.
216	
217	**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.
218	
219	**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.
220	
221	**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.
222	
223	**Related** — [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]; [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]]

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. ## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

# HSR/VHSR Delivery Shifts: Structured Repeats, Then Short Intervals, Then Small-Sided Games

**What it is** — Across the case studies, high-speed running (HSR/VHSR) volume is not just dosed up session to session, it is delivered through three successive formats as rehab advances. Early sessions accumulate HSR through structured, individually-prescribed repeats over a fixed distance (e.g. 100 m and 60 m repeats). From around mid-rehab (session 5 in Case 1, session 3 in Case 2), HSR shifts to short interval formats: "10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, or 15 seconds on and off" (Case 1, ~10:17-10:35), and "short interval, high intensity interval training formats, like 10 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 20 seconds on, 20 seconds off" (Case 2, ~23:14-23:22). From around session 7-8, small-sided games and technical/tactical drills start to contribute HSR/VHSR "a little bit more meaningfully" or "more organically," alongside whatever prescribed running work continues (Case 1, ~10:35-10:46; Case 2, ~23:25-23:30). A similar shift to small-sided games shows up in Case 4, a knee-joint case kept straight-line-only through session 6 for bracing reasons: "small-sided games, so modified rehab specific drills and also partial participation with the team" began at session 8 (~41:34-41:40). Harries reports a separate, linear VHSR/sprint increase from sessions 4-8 in the same passage (~41:43-41:46) without explicitly linking the two statements, so this case supports the format shift itself but not a stated causal link to VHSR volume.

**Why it works** — Harries does not give an explicit mechanism for why the delivery format itself should shift (his only nearby general statement is that session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding," said of the mid-rehab checkpoint, not this format shift specifically, ~20:08-20:14). Inference (entry writer's): moving from individually-prescribed, fixed-distance repeats to short intervals to game-based drills lets the athlete accumulate the same category of high-speed exposure in progressively less predictable, more sport-representative contexts, without needing to represcribe every rep once basic mechanics and pacing are established.

**When to apply** — Use as the default organizing structure for programming HSR/VHSR volume across an on-field rehab block, once basic linear mechanics and pacing are established (roughly Level 1-2, see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]). Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP protocol of its own yet; this three-stage shift is a directly transferable structure to pair with Baylor's own GPS velocity-band thresholds.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed session-count rule; the session numbers cited here (5, 3, 7, 8) are case-specific, not a stated formula, and the source's own repeated caveat is that the framework is a guide adjusted to context, not a step-by-step protocol (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]). The Case 4 example also shows the shift can run alongside other, unrelated restrictions (change-of-direction was still withheld through session 6 there for bracing reasons); do not treat "small-sided games by session 7-8" as evidence that all restrictions lift on that same timeline. Do not import a specific case's session numbers as a prescription.

**Example** — In [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]], HSR moved from 100 m repeats (session 2, which overshot the low 17 km/h threshold, see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]) to short intervals (session 3) to small-sided games contributing HSR organically (session 8).

**Related** — [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]; [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]]; [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]; [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]]

# Fitting Rehab Sessions Into the Team's Own Training Week

**What it is** — As a returning athlete moves from an isolated running-only schedule into overlapping with team training, Harries shapes each week of rehab around the team's own weekly training rhythm, not a fixed rehab-only calendar. Case 2: "by week three, we started to fall into the team's training structure a bit more" (~17:40-17:44): a small on-field rehab session early in the week, a return to partial training midweek, then "a larger combined rehab session with modified team training" at week's end (~17:45-17:56). Case 2, week 4: two non-consecutive training days then two consecutive days, the second-to-last being "a captain's run walkthrough style session, though very low intensity," followed by return to play in a match (~17:56-18:10). Case 1, week 3: "a high moderate high structure, including partial training exposure in the midweek, and a heavier modified training session on the weekend" (~05:18-05:27). Case 1, week 4: "one light partial session, a full training midweek, and a walkthrough style session... And then they played their game at the end of the week" (~05:27-05:37). Case 4 (knee), week 5: running frequency was deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions "in order to make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions," explicitly to bridge into the larger session planned at the end of week 6 (~37:24-37:46). Case 4, week 7 (the RTP week): "a small session early in the week, a moderate session mid-week, which was aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season," then return to play at week's end (~38:13-38:26).

**Why it works** — For the Case 4 frequency cut, Harries states the reason directly: reducing running frequency let him "make a more significant volume increase in those individual sessions" so there was "a nice little progression into" the larger, match-comparable session planned for the following week (~37:26-37:55). For the broader practice of shaping rehab-week structure around the team's rhythm, his only stated reason is the week-7 mid-week session "aligning to the team's normal training schedule in the in-season" (~38:20-38:22); he gives no further explicit rationale for the general practice. Inference (entry writer's): tying rehab-session load to the team's own hard/light day pattern lets the returning athlete's tolerance build in step with what full training will actually demand in the week he returns, rather than on a schedule disconnected from it.

**When to apply** — When designing a returning athlete's week once he is off an isolated running-only schedule and beginning to overlap with team sessions (typically mid-to-late rehab, alongside modified/partial training participation). Eric's review: Applied Performance "already undulate[s] load across the team week," and this pattern is proposed as "the same logic applied to one returning player, anchored to the team's Tue/Wed high, Thu low pattern" (Review and Plan, line 75) - i.e. the existing team-week undulation is the natural anchor for this on-field-rehab pattern, not a separate structure to invent.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries never states this as a fixed template; no claim is made that a "high-moderate-high" week or a captain's-run walkthrough is required, and the specific weekly shapes differ across all three cases that show them, tracking each athlete's own timeline and injury type. None of it is validated against outcome data beyond what happened in each case being reported without a stated recurrence. Do not import a specific case's weekly pattern wholesale as a template; use the underlying idea, build the rehab week around the team's actual week, and rebuild the specific days for each returning athlete.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], weeks 5-7, for the clearest stated rationale: a frequency cut used as a deliberate bridge to a larger session, and an RTP week deliberately matched to the team's normal in-season training rhythm.

**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]; [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]]; [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]] (a different, injury-driven reason to cut frequency in Case 3, distinct from this team-week bridging reason in Case 4)

# The Mid-Rehab Checkpoint: ~85% MV Around Day 10-14 for Hamstring-Type Injuries

**What it is** — Harries gives a calendar anchor, matched to force-production, reactive-strength and healing-time criteria that line up with the general 75-85% MV gate (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]), for hamstring-type strain injuries specifically. Describing session 5 (stated as "identical to session five in case one," ~19:47-19:56), he says it "probably represents a typical mid stage max velocity progression for this type of injury at about the 10 [to] 14 day post injury mark" (~19:56-20:04) and, discussing the same session a few lines later, that it "typifies the point in rehab where you push towards around about 85% max velocity at that day 14 type mark, plus or minus, but rarely would you go beyond that. Most would consider this a bit of a sound ceiling until further force production or reactive strength criteria are confirmed, as well as some adequate time for biological healing" (~20:40-21:02). He adds that the session structure "could be employed slightly earlier or held slightly later, depending on how the athlete's responding" (~20:08-20:14). The transcript literally reads "10 day 14 post injury mark," almost certainly an ASR-dropped "to"; read as "10 to 14 day."

**Why it works** — Same underlying rationale as the general gate: Harries treats ~85% MV as a workable interim ceiling pending confirmation of force-production and reactive-strength criteria, plus adequate healing time, not as evidence that higher intensity would be unsafe. He gives no physiological mechanism for why day 10-14 specifically is the natural point for this pause; the timing is presented as his stated clinical experience ("most would consider," "typical"), not a derived rule.

**When to apply** — As a rough calendar anchor for planning when a hamstring-type strain rehab should reach the 75-85% MV gate, so force-production and reactive-strength testing (Nordic, isometric benchmarks, hop test; see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]) can be scheduled around day 10-14 rather than left open-ended. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that Baylor has no documented phased RTP timeline of its own yet; this gives a starting calendar reference to validate against Baylor's own returning-athlete data.

**When NOT to apply** — This is stated for "this type of injury," meaning the hamstring-type strains of Cases 1-2. Harries treats the calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]], discussed later in the same module, ~27:00 onward) as a deliberately different, lower-frequency injury pattern; do not apply the day-10-14 anchor to that case, or to a joint/ligament case such as [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]], which was still brace-restricted and straight-line-only through session 6. This is expert opinion ("most would consider"), not a validated cutoff. # The Five-Element Case-Review Structure

**What it is** — Harries reviews each of his four case studies through the same five elements, stated explicitly: "the rehab timeline, which is a high-level overview of the return to play calendar"; "the loading structure. So how was loading planned and how was it progressed across on-field rehab"; "the progression of maximum velocity and how those linear running intensities were increased"; "our multi-directional speed and agility progressions and how we developed acceleration, deceleration and change of direction"; and "for each case study... the sport-specific skill progressions and how the technical and tactical tasks were integrated" (~00:39-01:17). He also states the cases were deliberately chosen to minimize individual complexity so the framework's application would read clearly, while acknowledging "no case is ever entirely free from complexity" (~01:21-01:45), and that he included cases that "didn't go perfect to show that the real world is not always that way" (~01:45-01:51).

**Why it works** — No stated mechanism; this is a presentation and documentation structure Harries uses for teaching, not a claim about rehab physiology or efficacy.

**When to apply** — As a template for a Baylor RTP case log or after-action review: for a returning athlete, record (1) the RTP timeline/calendar, (2) the loading structure and how it was progressed, (3) max-velocity progression, (4) MDSA progression, and (5) sport-skill progression. Eric's baseline: `method-baseline.md` records that standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates "do not yet exist" at Applied Performance and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work; this five-element structure is a ready-made scaffold specifically for RTP case documentation, distinct from that broader reporting gap.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a presentation structure built for four selected, deliberately simplified cases, not a validated clinical documentation standard, and Harries does not claim it captures everything relevant to an actual RTP decision. It has no explicit slot for the competitive-exposure/hesitation criteria in [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] and [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]] (those show up folded into the sport-skill-progression element in practice, not as their own listed element). Do not treat the five elements as exhaustive without adding Baylor's own required documentation fields (medical clearance sign-off, testing-battery results, incident/mechanism detail) alongside them.

**Example** — Each of the four case-study entries in this folder roughly follows this order in its own body sections (rehab timeline folded into "What it is," then MV progression, MDSA, sport-specific skill as separate paragraphs), though none names the structure explicitly and none gives "loading structure" its own separate paragraph the way Harries' five-element list implies; see [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for the closest match.

**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]; [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] (reciprocal link suggestion: each could add "documented using [[framework--five-element-case-review-structure]]" to its own Related line)

# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase

**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).

**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Harries' own stated reason is narrower: the middle-phase time is set "to equate to a given speed through that middle distance... that's going to correspond to the athlete's max velocity" (~18:18-18:29) - i.e. it gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity.

**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.

**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.

**Related** — [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]; [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]]

lines: **When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example, what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

-**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise — see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise: see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02), the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

**When to apply** — Whenever a metric is being tracked at both a daily/weekly cadence and used to make phase-level claims about program effectiveness. **Eric's baseline:** the baseline states a preference for weekly tracking over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early [method-baseline.md, Testing and assessment]. **Inference:** this is a real tension worth naming: Weber's framework would say that weekly cadence is monitoring (a status/trend check), and it still needs a separate, phase-block comparison to answer the testing question of whether the athlete actually improved. The two are not substitutes for each other even when the same test (e.g., daily CMJ for mRSI) feeds both.

-**When NOT to apply** — Inference: single-number illustrations in the course, such as the 12% RFD change Weber dismisses as "well inside our range of variability with the MDC" (Lab 2E transcript 00:04:08 to 00:04:24), are local examples, not transferable thresholds; the lesson summary adds the same caveat (see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]). **Example** — Weber's decision-matrix template: "if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point," worked through for an eccentric-knee-flexor-force drop (confirm test quality/re-test, physio screen and ROM checks, adjust exposure plan, reassess immediately and at 24 hours, progress only when stable) (p.2).

**When to apply** — Any time staff turnover occurs on a testing team, a vendor pushes a software update that changes default settings, or a test is handed from one tester to another without a written procedure to follow. **Eric's baseline:** the current CMJ family runs a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol on ForceDecks [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring], which is the kind of documented procedure this principle argues protects comparability. **Eric's baseline:** Eric's own corpus also shows two protocol documents giving different cueing instructions for the same CMJ test, the Assessment Manual says "do not coach the strategy of jumping," while Force Plate Testing V3 gives specific verbal cues [method-baseline.md Tensions #5]. **Inference:** two written protocols giving different cueing for the same test (Tension #5), one possibly legacy (Tension #4), is the documentation-side version of protocol drift: the fix is to retire or reconcile one document so staff cannot run the same-named test two ways.

-**When NOT to apply** — This principle addresses procedural consistency, not whether the test itself is the right one to run. **Inference:** a perfectly standardized bad test is still a bad test (see [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]). content.content:
**Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed and there has been adequate time for biological healing (~21:00). Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.

24:**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 3-5: low-intensity technical actions (stationary kicking/handball), then controlled movement. From session 6: positional-specific drills under fatigue (volume/technical output under load). Sessions 8-10: competitive play in modified small-sided formats (3v2 handball), increasing decision-making demand. Full training at session 10 included large-group competitive play under near-match conditions.
26:**Why it works** — This is Harries' example of a grade 2 injury run against a compressed, late-season timeline; every design choice (linear-then-undulating, HSR via short intervals from session 5, sport-skill drills carrying more of the late HSR load) reflects deliberately trading off ideal dosage against a hard return-date constraint.
